endorsements.quote: Prospective, real-world evaluations—such as controlled interrupted time series or (cluster) randomized controlled trials (RCTs)—that assess patient safety outcomes (eg, delayed diagnoses and avoidable emergency use), workflow effects, and override behaviors in GP practice are urgently needed.
This means disaggregating performance (TPR, FPR, and calibration) by age, ethnicity, language, deprivation, and their multidimensional aspects to identify and mitigate differential risks.
AI triage requires continuous monitoring, with statistically principled detection of drift, subgroup miscalibration, and emerging hazards [ 63 ].

Operationally, this requires three commitments: (1) prospective, real-world evaluations in GP; (2) equity-stratified performance reporting guided by frameworks, such as PROGRESS-Plus; and (3) rigorous postmarket surveillance with drift and subgroup monitoring and WHO International Classification for Patient Safety–aligned incident reporting.
In practice, these can be operationalized by setting thresholds (eg, sensitivity gaps ≤5% between groups), with breaches triggering model review and corrective action.
Alternative frameworks, such as the health equity impact assessment tool, as seen in Textbox 1 , are used prospectively to anticipate equity impacts before interventions are deployed [ 52 ].

Operationally, this requires three commitments: (1) prospective, real-world evaluations in GP; (2) equity-stratified performance reporting guided by frameworks, such as PROGRESS-Plus; and (3) rigorous postmarket surveillance with drift and subgroup monitoring and WHO International Classification for Patient Safety–aligned incident reporting.
For each subgroup, TPRs should be reported with measures of uncertainty (eg, 95% CIs or standard errors), particularly where subgroup sample sizes are small.

Without governance mechanisms, such as version control, audit logs, safety dashboards, and periodic revalidation, performance may degrade over time as populations, language, and risk profiles change [ 32 ].

unlisted_practices: Evaluate AI triage as a sociotechnical intervention, examining how clinicians interpret, override, or trust AI suggestions and how it fits workflow.

Design AI triage explanations to be workflow-integrated and low burden, with main escalation drivers, uncertainty indicators, override-required prompts for high-risk edge cases, and consistent safety-netting text.
Ensure AI explanations are stable so that near-identical inputs do not produce inconsistent rationales.
Use causal evaluation designs such as interrupted time series, RCTs, propensity score methods, instrumental variables, or target trial emulation to attribute safety effects to AI deployment.
Report equity-stratified performance across intersectional subgroups (e.g., age×ethnicity, ethnicity×deprivation) using frameworks such as PROGRESS-Plus.
Adopt governance frameworks such as people, process, technology, and operations to structure oversight of AI triage.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint/commentary paper arguing for safer, more equitable real-world evidence, governance, and postmarket surveillance of AI triage in primary care.
